lessons.title: Lesson 1: Planning your school week
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Turn a messy list of tasks into a simple weekly plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given your tasks, due dates and fixed times for the week, you will make a simple weekly plan with AI and change it to fit your real life, with the hardest work first, breaks, and the plan copied into a planner or calendar.
School, practice, clubs, a part-time job, chores and friends all compete for your time. An AI assistant can help you put it in order if you give it the facts.
List what is due and when, plus your fixed times like practice or work. Then ask: "Here is my week. Make a simple plan with study time each day, the hardest work first, and breaks. Keep it to one screen."
The plan is a draft. Move things around until it fits your real life, then put it in a planner, Google Calendar or your school's calendar app.
Step by step:
- Write down every task and due date.
- Add fixed times: classes, practice, work, family.
- Ask AI to make a simple weekly plan with breaks.
- Change it to fit you, then copy it into your planner or calendar.
Words to know:
- Due date: the day work must be handed in.
- Prioritize: decide what to do first because it matters most or is due soonest.
Try it now: List everything due this week and your fixed times. Ask an AI assistant you are allowed to use to make a simple weekly plan. Change one thing to fit your life, and copy it into a planner or calendar.
You can now build a realistic weekly plan with AI's help.

check.q: What are "fixed times" when you plan your week?
options: Times you cannot move, like classes, practice or work
Times the AI picks for you
check.why: Fixed times are commitments the plan must fit around.

check.q: AI's plan puts study time during your shift at work. What do you do?
options: Move the study time to fit your real schedule
Ask AI to cancel your shift
check.why: The AI plan is a draft; you change it to fit your real life.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Breaking a big project into small steps
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Split a big assignment into small steps with dates.
This lesson builds toward: Given a big assignment and its due date, you will break the assignment into 30-minute steps with dates and check them against the teacher's rubric, finishing two days early with every required part included.
Big projects feel scary because they look like one huge thing. Breaking them into small steps makes them doable.
Give AI the assignment instructions (in your own words or pasted, with no private information) and the due date. Ask: "Break this into small steps I can do in 30 minutes each, with a date for each step, finishing two days early."
Read the steps and make sure they match what your teacher asked for. Your teacher's instructions and rubric always win over the AI's plan.
Step by step:
- Share the instructions and due date.
- Ask for 30-minute steps with dates.
- Ask it to finish two days early.
- Check the steps against your teacher's rubric.
Words to know:
- Rubric: the list your teacher uses to grade the work.
- Milestone: a small goal on the way to finishing a big one.
Try it now: Take one big assignment you have now or had recently. Ask AI to break it into 30-minute steps with dates. Check them against the instructions and fix any step that does not match.
You can now turn a big assignment into small dated steps.

check.q: Why ask AI to finish the steps two days early?
options: It leaves time for surprises or fixes
check.why: Finishing early gives you room if something takes longer than planned.

check.q: AI's steps skip the bibliography your teacher requires. What do you do?
options: Leave it out, since AI knows best
Add a step for it, because the teacher's instructions win
Ask a friend to do it
check.why: Your teacher's instructions and rubric always win over the AI's plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Understanding a hard reading
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI to understand a hard text while still reading it yourself.
This lesson builds toward: Given a hard paragraph from a class reading, you will read it yourself, ask AI to explain it and define hard words, then reread it, writing one correct sentence in your own words about its meaning.
Some readings are tough: old language, science words or long paragraphs. AI can help you understand them, as long as you still read the text.
Try this: read a paragraph first. Then ask AI: "Explain this paragraph in simple words" or "What do these 3 words mean?" or "Give me 3 questions to think about while I read."
A summary from AI can miss things or get them wrong, and it cannot replace reading for class. Use it to unlock the text, then go back and read again.
Step by step:
- Read the paragraph yourself first.
- Ask AI to explain it simply or define hard words.
- Ask for questions to guide your reading.
- Reread the paragraph with the new understanding.
Words to know:
- Summary: a short version of the main points.
- Context: the words and ideas around a word that help explain its meaning.
Try it now: Take one hard paragraph from a class reading. Read it, ask AI to explain it in simple words and define two hard words, then reread it and write one sentence in your own words about what it means.
You can now use AI to unlock a hard reading and then understand it yourself.

check.q: Why can't an AI summary replace doing the reading?
options: It can miss things or get them wrong
check.why: An AI summary can miss or get details wrong, so you still read the text.

check.q: You are stuck on a paragraph full of science words. What is the best first move?
options: Read it yourself, then ask AI what the hard words mean
Ask AI to summarize the whole book
Copy the AI summary into your notes
check.why: Read first, use AI to unlock the hard parts, then reread.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Getting feedback on your own writing
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Ask AI for feedback on a draft you wrote, then revise it yourself.
This lesson builds toward: Given a draft you wrote and your teacher's permission, you will ask AI for three things to improve instead of a rewrite, and revise the draft in your own words, with every change written by you.
Writing your own draft is where learning happens. AI can then act like a coach: it can point out unclear sentences, missing evidence or grammar mistakes.
Ask for feedback, not a rewrite: "Here is my paragraph. Do not rewrite it. Tell me 3 things to improve and why." Then you make the changes in your own words.
If your teacher does not allow AI feedback, use other help: a classmate, the school writing center, or your teacher during office hours.
Step by step:
- Write your own draft first.
- Check your teacher allows AI feedback.
- Ask for 3 things to improve, not a rewrite.
- Revise in your own words.
Words to know:
- Draft: an early version of your writing.
- Revise: improve your writing by changing ideas, order or words.
Try it now: Take a paragraph you wrote (if your teacher allows AI feedback). Ask for 3 things to improve without a rewrite. Make the changes yourself and compare the two versions.
You can now get feedback from AI and revise your own writing.

check.q: What does "feedback, not a rewrite" mean?
options: AI writes a new version for you
AI points out what to improve and you make the changes
check.why: Feedback tells you what to fix; you revise in your own words.

check.q: Your teacher does not allow AI feedback on this essay. What do you do?
options: Ask a classmate, the writing center or your teacher for feedback
Turn in the first draft without reading it
check.why: When AI is not allowed, other people can give you feedback.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Making a study plan for a test
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Build a day-by-day study plan and practice questions for a real test.
This lesson builds toward: Given a real test date, its topics and your daily time, you will build a day-by-day study plan with practice questions, answer them first and check them against your notes, spending more time on the questions you got wrong.
Cramming the night before usually does not work well. Studying a little each day and testing yourself does.
Tell AI the test date, the topics and how much time you have each day: "My biology test is Friday on cells and DNA. I have 30 minutes each day. Make a study plan with a practice quiz each day."
Ask for practice questions with the answers hidden, answer them yourself, then check against your notes or textbook. Spend more time on the questions you got wrong.
Step by step:
- Tell AI the test date, topics and your daily time.
- Ask for a day-by-day plan with practice.
- Answer practice questions before seeing answers.
- Check against your notes and focus on what you missed.
Words to know:
- Cramming: trying to learn everything right before a test.
- Spaced practice: studying a little over several days instead of all at once.
Try it now: Pick a real upcoming test. Ask AI for a day-by-day study plan using the time you really have. Do the first day's practice questions and check them against your notes.
You can now make a study plan and practice with AI for a real test.

check.q: What works better than cramming the night before?
options: Studying a little each day and testing yourself
check.why: Studying a little each day with self-tests helps you remember more.

check.q: You got 3 of 5 practice questions wrong on cell parts. What do you do next?
options: Move on to a new topic
Ask AI for the answers and memorize them
Spend more time on cell parts and check your notes
check.why: Focus your study time on what you missed.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Using AI honestly at school
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Follow your school's AI rules and say how you used AI.
This lesson builds toward: For any assignment where you might use AI, you will follow your teacher's AI rule, check any fact or source yourself, and write one line on how you used AI, handing in no AI-written work that is not allowed.
Schools have different AI rules. Some allow it for brainstorming and feedback, some want you to say when you used it, and some ban it for certain work. Your teacher's rule for that assignment is the one that counts.
Never hand in AI-written work as your own when it is not allowed. It can count as cheating, and you miss the learning. If AI helped, say how: "I used AI to make practice questions and to get feedback on my second paragraph."
AI can make up facts and sources. Never copy a quote or a book title from AI into your work without finding it yourself. Keep private information out of AI tools, and use your school account for school tools.
Step by step:
- Read your teacher's AI rule for this assignment.
- Use AI only in the ways allowed.
- Write one line saying how you used it.
- Check any fact or source yourself before using it.
Words to know:
- Academic integrity: being honest in schoolwork: what you hand in shows what you did.
- Cite: say where information came from.
Try it now: Final task: for a real test or project in the next two weeks, make a day-by-day study plan with AI, do 5 practice questions with hidden answers, check them against your notes, and write one line on how you followed your school's AI rules.
You can now use AI for school in ways that are allowed, honest and actually help you learn.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Study plan fits real life No plan, or it ignores classes, activities and work. A day-by-day plan up to the test date that fits around fixed times. The plan was changed after day one based on what was missed. Weekly time planning Study time is not on a calendar or planner. Study sessions are copied into a planner or calendar with breaks. The hardest topics are scheduled first in each session. Practice and checking Answers were looked at before trying, or not checked. Five practice questions answered first, then checked against notes. Wrong answers are listed with what to study more. Honest AI use No line on AI use, or AI was used in a way the teacher does not allow. One clear line on how AI was used, matching the teacher's rule. Also notes any fact or source from AI that was checked. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Whose AI rule counts for a particular assignment?
check.why: Schools differ, and your teacher's rule for that assignment is the one that counts.

check.q: AI gives you a great quote for your essay. What do you do before using it?
options: Find it in the real source yourself
Use it; AI does not make mistakes
check.why: AI can make up quotes and sources, so you find them yourself first.
